extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method, experimental philosophers, scientists learning inductive logic
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on four principal methods of induction (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, Residues) and on complications like plurality of causes and intermixture of effects for establishing causal relations from observation and experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish causation by comparing instances that are alike in all material circumstances except one antecedent; if the consequence follows when that antecedent is present and not when absent, that antecedent is implicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires taking pains to avoid accidental differences between paired cases (e.g., different pathological states of two legs of one animal). Repeat the experiment sufficiently often across different subjects to exclude the possibility that an abnormal circumstance is present in them all. Two instances (one positive, one negative) differing only in the antecedent are sufficient for a complete and rigorous induction in this method. Example: Brown-Séquard's experiments on paralysis where one leg was operated on and the other left healthy; repeated experiments across animals secure the method's conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer that a circumstance common to multiple instances is part of the cause when many instances (which differ otherwise) all present the same antecedent and the same consequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By itself, this method cannot prove causation; it yields suggestions that must be tested. When only a small number of instances are compared (e.g., two), agreement furnishes at most a slight probability because plurality of causes might mean the effect had different causes in different instances. The method gains strength only when the instances are indefinitely multiplied and varied yet continue to show the same association. Examples: observation that exhausted animals exhibit rapid putrefaction (many diverse cases agreeing in exhaustion). Simple everyday generalizations (e.g., 'dogs bark') are examples of this method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer a causal connection when systematic variations in one antecedent are accompanied by corresponding variations in the consequent (degree-dependent relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for establishing that the degree of an antecedent affects the degree of the effect. Example: Dr. Brown-Séquard's galvanic experiments where stronger electric charges produced a shorter duration of rigidity and more rapid putrefaction; the more powerful the charge, the more marked the effect. From such concomitant variations one may infer that the duration of rigidity depends on the degree of muscular irritability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues
rubrics_metrics.description: When the effects of all known causes are estimated and subtracted from an observed phenomenon, the remaining 'residual' phenomenon points to an unknown cause which should be investigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires that the effects of known causes be calculated or estimated and removed; the residual fact then suggests a new vera causa. Examples: residual anomalies in comet motion leading to hypotheses about a resisting medium; Arago's copper-plate experiment (retarding influence residual after accounting for air resistance and thread rigidity); Laplace's explanation of residual velocity in sound via heat developed by compression; detection of new chemical elements by examining concentrated residues. The method is particularly powerful in quantitative investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Method of Agreement and Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine Agreement and Difference to strengthen inferential claims: identify instances that agree in a circumstance and also instances where adding or removing that circumstance produces or removes the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The joint method can give inductive proof of a causal connection when the conditions are met. It is especially persuasive when the broader causal relation (e.g., that death causes rigidity and putrefaction) is already established by other evidence (Method of Difference), and then the joint method isolates which attendant circumstance of death determines variation in the effect. Example: cases showing that high muscular irritability (from good nutrition, rest, or cold) produce late and long-lived cadaveric rigidity, whereas low irritability (exhaustion, disease, convulsions) produce early and brief rigidity. The joint method helps show the irritability itself (not merely its causes) is the operative antecedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental control and repeatability (practical requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure experiments control for accidental differences and are repeated sufficiently to exclude abnormal or idiosyncratic conditions; reduce the chance that observed effects are due to uncontrolled factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume complete resemblance in all material circumstances without actively securing it—e.g., in paired experiments ensure both subjects are in comparable pathological conditions. Repeat experiments across different animals or subjects to prevent an abnormal circumstance from being present in all trials. These practices are necessary to secure the conditions of the Method of Difference and to lend credibility to inductive inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the same effect may be produced by several independent causes; one phenomenon may arise sometimes from A, sometimes from B, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fact undermines the reliability of the Method of Agreement when only a small number of instances are used: agreement in a single circumstance across two cases might be coincidental because different causes could produce the same effect. To address plurality of causes, multiply and vary instances: if many unlike cases all containing A produce the same effect, then either A is causal or the effect has as many different causes as there are instances; repeated varied confirmations strengthen the presumption in favor of A. The Method of Difference is not harmed by plurality of causes and remains reliable in isolating a cause from a matched positive/negative pair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermixture of Effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that effects of different causes may be homogeneous or mixed, lacking sharp boundaries between kinds of effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This complicates the analysis because different causes may produce not entirely distinct consequents but different portions or degrees of the same resultant phenomenon. Such intermixture increases the difficulty of separating causes and requires more careful analysis, often beyond simple Agreement comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of purely deductive/hypothetical approaches and need for inductive proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses and deduction aid discovery, but empirical hypotheses must be proved by inductive methods; induction needs tests analogous to the syllogistic test of deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be satisfied merely because a hypothesis is consistent with facts; induction requires active tests (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, Residues) to establish proof. Critics who deny the necessity of such tests mistake the nature of inductive evidence. Practical recommendation: use hypotheses to guide inquiry, but employ the four methods to test and secure empirical generalizations.
